title: In re A.K.M.
description: Whether the District Court violated a father's constitutional right to equal protection and due process by failing to advise him of his right to counsel and by not complying with mandatory notice-of-hearing provisions before terminating his parental rights.
plaintiff_argument: The guardians argued that the father never requested counsel, distinguishing prior cases, and that a generic mailing presumption should suffice for notice.
defendant_argument: The father argued his constitutional right to counsel was violated due to lack of advisal and appointment, and that the court failed to follow mandatory notice-of-hearing provisions of the Montana Adoption Act.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Montana reversed the District Court's orders terminating the father's parental rights and remanded the case with directions to ensure proper advisal of rights and compliance with statutory notice requirements.

title: State v. Cole
description: Whether the District Court legally imposed the $5,000-minimum fine mandated by § 61-8-731(1)(a)(iii), MCA (2019), when it suspended the portion Cole could not pay.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the District Court legally imposed the $5,000-minimum fine by suspending the portion Cole could not pay, and that the precedent of Gibbons should be overruled as manifestly wrong.
defendant_argument: Cole argued that the mandatory minimum fine is facially unconstitutional under the Excessive Fines clauses if he lacks the ability to pay, and that suspension of the fine cannot cure its constitutional infirmity.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the District Court's decision, holding that the mandatory minimum fine was legally imposed because the District Court conducted an ability-to-pay analysis and suspended the portion Cole was unable to pay.

title: Kalarchik v. State
description: Whether State Policies restricting the amendment of sex designation on birth certificates and driver's licenses for transgender individuals violate constitutional rights, with plaintiffs arguing they do and defendants arguing they do not.
plaintiff_argument: The State Policies violate the Montana Constitution's guarantees of equal protection, right to privacy, and prohibition against compelled speech by preventing transgender individuals from amending their birth certificates and driver's licenses to reflect their gender identity, while cisgender individuals can correct errors.
defendant_argument: The State Policies are necessary to maintain accurate vital records, further health and research efforts, and protect women's rights by defining sex biologically. The policies do not discriminate based on sex as they apply equally to all individuals, allowing amendments only for clerical errors in birth sex, not for gender identity changes.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the District Court's preliminary injunction, preventing the State from enforcing the State Policies as they pertain to amending birth certificates and driver's licenses.

title: Kendrick v. Knudsen
description: Whether Ballot Issue 8 (BI-8) violates the separate vote requirement of Article XIV, Section 11, of the Montana Constitution and whether the Attorney General had the authority to append a fiscal statement to BI-8.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that BI-8 constitutes a single constitutional amendment establishing and safeguarding the fundamental right to initiative and referendum, and that the Attorney General lacked authority to append a fiscal statement because there was no fiscal impact.
defendant_argument: The Attorney General argued that BI-8 violates the separate-vote requirement by proposing multiple, unrelated constitutional changes, including imposing judicial deadlines, restricting government resource use, and creating statute-like criteria, and that he had authority to append a fiscal statement due to potential litigation costs.
decision_outcome: The court granted the petition, reversed the Attorney General's legal-sufficiency determination, struck the fiscal statement, and ordered the Attorney General to prepare ballot statements.

title: In the Matter of Austin Miles Knudsen
description: Whether the Commission on Practice's discipline of the Attorney General for alleged violations of the Montana Rules of Professional Conduct in the course of his elected official duties violates the separation of powers under the Montana Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Attorney General is subject to professional conduct rules like any other attorney, and his conduct violated several rules, thus discipline does not violate separation of powers.
defendant_argument: Disciplining him for official actions violates the separation of powers by allowing the Court to judge his executive office, and his actions were justified as an open refusal or protected speech.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed the disciplinary case against Austin Miles Knudsen due to due process violations by the Commission on Practice, despite finding that Knudsen violated some professional conduct rules.

title: State v. Alford
description: Whether the mandatory minimum custodial sentences required by Montana's felony DUI statutes for multiple offenses are unconstitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that Alford waived his right to appeal and that the mandatory minimum custodial sentences are constitutional, distinguishing them from the fines found unconstitutional in Gibbons.
defendant_argument: Alford argues that the mandatory minimum custodial sentence for felony DUI is unconstitutional, violating the Cruel and Unusual Punishment Clause, similar to how mandatory minimum fines were found unconstitutional in Gibbons.
decision_outcome: The District Court did not err in imposing the statutory minimum custodial sentence for Alford's fourth DUI, and the Supreme Court affirmed the decision.

title: Montanans Against Irresponsible Densification v. State
description: Whether the Montana Land Use Planning Act (MLUPA) and other housing reform bills violate Montanans' constitutional right to participate in site-specific land use decisions and the right to equal protection, and whether these laws can supersede more restrictive private covenants.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Montanans Against Irresponsible Densification, LLC (MAID), argued that the MLUPA unconstitutionally limits public participation in site-specific land use decisions, and that the housing reform statutes violate equal protection by unfairly burdening homeowners not protected by private restrictive covenants and by arbitrarily classifying communities based on population. MAID also claimed the laws could not supersede more restrictive private covenants.
defendant_argument: The defendants (State of Montana, Shelter WF, Inc., and Montana League of Cities and Towns) argued that the MLUPA's public participation provisions are constitutional, emphasizing participation at earlier planning stages, and that MAID failed to prove equal protection violations because the alleged classes were not similarly situated. They also contended that the claim regarding private restrictive covenants was non-justiciable.
decision_outcome: The court found MAID's challenge justiciable, concluded that the MLUPA's public participation laws are not facially unconstitutional, affirmed that MAID failed to establish equal protection violations, and vacated the District Court's declaratory judgment on private restrictive covenants as an advisory opinion.

title: Montanans for Nonpartisan Courts v. Knudsen
description: Whether the Attorney General's revised ballot statement for Constitutional Initiative 132 (CI-132) is compliant with statutory requirements, or if Montanans for Nonpartisan Courts' (MNC) proposed statement is compliant.
plaintiff_argument: MNC argued the Attorney General's revised statement was argumentative, misleading, and prejudicial, and that their own proposed statement was statutorily and constitutionally compliant.
defendant_argument: The Attorney General argued his revised statement corrected misleading language about the constitutional status quo and informed voters about the meaning of "nonpartisan," and that MNC's statement was deficient for not reflecting the current constitution and failing to define "nonpartisan."
decision_outcome: The court rejected the Attorney General's revised statement and certified Montanans for Nonpartisan Courts' proposed ballot statement for Constitutional Initiative 132.

title: City of Kalispell v. Doman
description: Whether Sean Doman's actions of filming a traffic stop and refusing to move constituted obstruction of a peace officer, and whether the application of the obstruction statute violated his free speech rights.
plaintiff_argument: The City argued that Doman obstructed officers by creating a safety risk and diverting their attention, and that his constitutional arguments were not properly preserved for appeal.
defendant_argument: Doman argued his conviction was not supported by sufficient evidence, the obstruction statute was unconstitutional as applied, he was exercising his First Amendment right to film police, and he did not knowingly obstruct officers.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Sean Doman's conviction for obstructing a peace officer.

title: Netzer v. State
description: Whether House Bill 702, which prohibits discrimination based on vaccination status, violates the Montana Constitution's single-subject and clear-title requirements, and whether the District Court erred in its procedural handling of Netzer's constitutional claims.
plaintiff_argument: Netzer argued that HB 702 violated various constitutional rights, including inalienable rights, environmental duties, equal protection, unenumerated rights, and the single-subject and clear-title requirements of the Montana Constitution, and that the District Court erred procedurally by barring litigation of constitutional claims on the merits.
defendant_argument: The State argued that HB 702 is constitutional, that the District Court's review should be formulaic, and that Subsection (4) is germane to the bill's title, and cross-appealed the District Court's invalidation of Subsection (4).
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the dismissal of Netzer's constitutional claims, upheld the constitutionality of § 49-2-312(1) of HB 702, and reversed the District Court's ruling to uphold the constitutionality of § 49-2-312(4) of HB 702.

title: State v. Herzog
description: Whether the District Court relied on clearly erroneous findings of fact when it denied Herzog's motion to suppress, with the plaintiff arguing that the denial was proper due to sufficient particularized suspicion, and the defendant arguing that the denial was improper because Detective Holzer lacked sufficient particularized suspicion.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Detective Holzer had sufficient particularized suspicion to conduct the stop, and therefore the District Court's denial of Herzog's motion to suppress was correct.
defendant_argument: Herzog argued that Detective Holzer lacked sufficient particularized suspicion to initiate the stop that led to her arrest, and that the District Court relied on clearly erroneous findings of fact when denying her motion to suppress.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the District Court's denial of Herzog's motion to suppress, finding that the District Court did not rely on clearly erroneous findings of fact.

title: Montana Environmental Information Center v. Office of the Governor
description: Whether a party who successfully vindicates their right to know under the Montana Constitution is entitled to a presumption towards awarding attorney's fees, and whether such fees are mandatory or discretionary in a mandamus action.
plaintiff_argument: MEIC argued that successfully enforcing the constitutional right to know is a public service, warranting a presumption for attorney's fees, and that 'may recover' in mandamus statutes implies mandatory fees if requested.
defendant_argument: The Governor's Office argued that attorney's fees are discretionary, they did not act in bad faith or with unreasonable delay, and the information could have been obtained through discovery. They also argued that a mandatory mandamus award conflicts with discretionary remedies under the Public Records Act.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the District Court's denial of attorney's fees and remanded the case, establishing a rebuttable presumption towards awarding attorney's fees for plaintiffs who successfully enforce their constitutional right to know.

title: Montana Environmental Information Center & Sierra Club v. Montana Department of Environmental Quality
description: Whether the Montana Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) adequately analyzed lighting impacts and greenhouse gas emissions in its environmental review for an air quality permit for a natural-gas-fueled power plant.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that DEQ failed to take a "hard look" at the gas plant's lighting impacts and greenhouse gas emissions, and that MEPA requires DEQ to analyze GHG emissions as part of its air quality permitting process.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that DEQ performed a sufficient analysis of lighting impacts, that MEPA does not require DEQ to analyze GHG emissions, and that the District Court erred in vacating the permit without making specific findings.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the District Court's ruling that DEQ adequately analyzed noise impacts and that DEQ must analyze GHG emissions and conduct additional review on lighting impacts, but reversed the District Court's order vacating the permit, reinstating it and remanding for further MEPA analysis.

title: Montana Trout Unlimited v. Montana Department of Natural Resources & Conservation
description: Whether the Montana Water Use Act requires a beneficial use permit for mine dewatering water that is not applied to a beneficial use.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Montana Trout Unlimited (MTU), argued that mine dewatering, even if not explicitly a "waste," must be considered a "beneficial use" under the MWUA and therefore requires a permit, or that the MWUA's exclusion of it from permitting creates an unconstitutional loophole that undermines comprehensive water regulation.
defendant_argument: The defendants, Montana Department of Natural Resources and Conservation (DNRC) and Tintina Montana, Inc., argued that mine dewatering, when not applied to a beneficial use, is neither a beneficial use nor a waste under the MWUA, and thus falls outside the Act's permitting process, consistent with long-standing agency interpretation and other environmental regulations.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the District Court's decision, which upheld the Department of Natural Resources and Conservation's (DNRC) determination that mine dewatering not put to beneficial use does not require a permit under the Montana Water Use Act.

title: Cottonwood Environmental Law Center v. State
description: Whether Section 7-5-131(2)(f), MCA (2023), which limits the right of local citizen initiatives to regulate "auxiliary containers," is facially unconstitutional under Article XI, Section 8, of the Montana Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that Section 7-5-131(2)(f), MCA, is unconstitutional because it impermissibly restricts the constitutional right of local citizen initiatives to regulate "auxiliary containers."
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the Legislature has the authority to limit the powers of local government, including local initiative powers, and therefore Section 7-5-131(2)(f), MCA, is constitutional.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the District Court's decision, ruling that Section 7-5-131(2)(f), MCA, is constitutional and that the Montana Constitution's limits on local self-government powers also apply to local initiative powers.

title: O’Neil v. Gianforte
description: Whether Montana law recognizes a privilege exception to Article II, Section 9, of the Montana Constitution that shields from public disclosure information the Governor receives during pre-decisional deliberations.
plaintiff_argument: O'Neill argued that the Governor's pre-decisional deliberation information (ABMs) should be publicly disclosed under the right to know, and no executive privilege should shield it.
defendant_argument: Governor Gianforte argued that an executive privilege exists under Montana law to shield pre-decisional deliberation information (ABMs) from public disclosure to ensure candid advice and uphold separation of powers.
decision_outcome: The court reversed in part and affirmed in part the lower court's decision, recognizing a gubernatorial privilege under Montana law but affirming that the Governor's claims of privilege are subject to in camera review.

title: Planned Parenthood of Montana v. State (Planned Parenthood 1)
description: Whether three laws passed by the 2021 Montana Legislature, regulating abortion, violate Montana's constitutional guarantees of individual privacy, equal protection, and free speech.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs, Planned Parenthood of Montana, argued that the challenged laws (HB 136, HB 140, and HB 171) are unconstitutional as they infringe upon the rights to privacy, equal protection, and free speech, and are not supported by medically acknowledged bona fide health risks.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the State of Montana, argued that the laws are constitutional, serve compelling state interests such as mitigating fetal pain and protecting women's health, and are narrowly tailored to achieve these interests.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the District Court's order, declaring HB 136, HB 140, and HB 171 unconstitutional and permanently enjoining their enforcement.

title: Cross v. State
description: Whether Senate Bill 99 (SB 99), which bans gender-affirming care for minors, violates the constitutional rights of minors and healthcare providers in Montana.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that SB 99 infringes upon their fundamental rights to privacy and equal protection under the Montana Constitution, and that the gender-affirming treatments proscribed by the bill are safe, effective, and medically necessary for minors with gender dysphoria.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that SB 99 is necessary to protect minors from harmful, experimental puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones, and irreversible surgical procedures, asserting a lack of medical consensus on gender-affirming care for minors.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the District Court's grant of a preliminary injunction, temporarily enjoining the enforcement of Senate Bill 99.

title: Planned Parenthood of Montana v. State (Planned Parenthood 3)
description: Whether the District Court manifestly abused its discretion by granting a preliminary injunction which enjoined HB 544, HB 862, and the Rule.
plaintiff_argument: The Providers argued that HB 544, HB 862, and the Rule are unconstitutional because they infringe on the right to privacy and equal protection by restricting access to abortion services for Medicaid-eligible patients.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the provisions are legitimate funding measures, not restrictions on constitutional rights, and should be reviewed under a rational basis test, and that the Providers lacked standing.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the District Court's preliminary injunction, enjoining HB 544, HB 862, and the Rule.

title: Planned Parenthood of Montana v. State (Planned Parenthood 4)
description: Whether the District Court manifestly abused its discretion by granting a preliminary injunction which enjoined HB 575 and HB 721, two laws regarding abortion.
plaintiff_argument: The Providers argued that both HB 575 and HB 721 are unconstitutional as they infringe upon the right to privacy under the Montana Constitution, are not narrowly tailored to address a bona fide health risk, and HB 575 imposes medically unnecessary ultrasound requirements, while HB 721 bans the only outpatient abortion procedure after 15 weeks LMP.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the Providers lacked standing, and that neither HB 575 nor HB 721 violates the right to privacy, contending the bills are subject to rational basis review or, if strict scrutiny applies, they withstand it as they do not infringe on the right to a lawful pre-viability abortion and HB 575 only requires an ultrasound to determine fetal viability.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the District Court's preliminary injunction, thereby enjoining HB 575 and HB 721.

title: Acorn International v. State
description: Whether the Secretary of State's fees for accessing the Montana voter file are lawful under state statute and the NVRA, and whether the Secretary violated the 'right to know' under the Montana Constitution by failing to provide documentation of the actual costs.
plaintiff_argument: ACORN argued that the Secretary's fees for the voter file were 'unreasonably large' and not justified by the 'actual cost' of reproducing the voter file, violating Montana statute and the NVRA. They also claimed the Secretary violated the 'right to know' by not providing documentation of these costs.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the Secretary's fees were lawful, set by administrative rule, and represented a reasonable portion of the annual costs to maintain the voter file, thus not conflicting with the NVRA. They also contended that the 'right to know' was not violated because ACORN's initial request for documentation was not specific enough.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the District Court's ruling that the Secretary's fees for access to the Montana voter file are lawful and do not conflict with the NVRA, and that the Secretary did not violate ACORN's constitutional 'right to know' because ACORN's record request did not specifically request the documents it alleged were withheld.

title: State v. Case
description: Whether the District Court erred in denying Case's motion to suppress evidence obtained from a warrantless home entry and whether it abused its discretion in denying a new trial based on an alleged Brady violation.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the warrantless entry was justified under the community caretaker doctrine due to exigent circumstances and that no Brady violation occurred, thus the District Court's decisions were correct.
defendant_argument: Case argued that the warrantless entry violated his Fourth Amendment rights and that the State committed a Brady violation by not disclosing exculpatory evidence, warranting a new trial.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the District Court's denial of Case's motion to suppress evidence from a warrantless entry and its denial of a new trial, finding the entry justified under the community caretaker doctrine and no Brady violation.

title: Planned Parenthood of Montana v. State of Montana (Planned Parenthood 2)
description: Whether the Parental Consent for Abortion Act of 2013, which requires parental consent or judicial waiver for minors seeking abortions, violates the Montana Constitution's fundamental rights of privacy and equal protection.
plaintiff_argument: The Parental Consent for Abortion Act of 2013 violates minors' fundamental rights to privacy and equal protection under the Montana Constitution by infringing on their right to abortion access without being narrowly tailored to a compelling state interest.
defendant_argument: The Parental Consent for Abortion Act of 2013 serves compelling state interests in protecting minors from sexual victimization, ensuring their psychological and physical wellbeing, guarding against immature decisions, and promoting parental rights, with the judicial bypass provision adequately respecting privacy and abortion access.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the Parental Consent for Abortion Act of 2013 violates a minor's fundamental right to control their body and destiny under the Montana Constitution, as it lacks adequate justification and does not enhance the protection of minors.

title: Held v. Montana
description: Whether the Montana Constitution's guarantee of a “clean and healthful environment” includes a stable climate system that sustains human lives and liberties, and whether the MEPA limitation is unconstitutional under this right.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Montana Constitution's fundamental right to a clean and healthful environment includes a stable climate system, and the MEPA Limitation (prohibiting review of GHG emissions) unconstitutionally violates this right.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the MEPA Limitation is constitutional, that the right to a clean and healthful environment does not encompass a stable climate system, that plaintiffs lacked standing, and that Montana's actions alone would not significantly impact global climate change.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the District Court's ruling, declaring the MEPA Limitation (§ 75-1-201(2)(a), MCA) and § 75-1-201(6)(a)(ii), MCA, unconstitutional, permanently enjoining their enforcement, and affirming that the right to a clean and healthful environment includes a stable climate system.

title: Montanans for Election Reform Action Fund v. Knudsen
description: Whether the Attorney General correctly concluded that Montanans for Election Reform's proposed ballot issue (BI-12) is legally insufficient because it violates the separate-vote requirement of Article XIV, Section 11, of the Montana Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Montanans for Election Reform, argued that the Attorney General's determination of legal insufficiency was incorrect, asserting that the proposed ballot issue's components are closely related and do not violate the separate-vote requirement.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the Attorney General, argued that the proposed ballot issue (BI-12) is legally insufficient because it proposes multiple, unrelated constitutional amendments, thereby violating the separate-vote requirement of the Montana Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court held that the Attorney General erred in concluding that the proposed ballot issue was legally insufficient and granted the petition for declaratory judgment, ordering the Attorney General to prepare a ballot statement.

title: Forward Montana v. State
description: Whether it was an abuse of discretion for the District Court to deny Appellants' attorney fees under the private attorney general doctrine, with the plaintiffs arguing it was an abuse of discretion given their successful constitutional challenge, and the defendant arguing it was not an abuse of discretion and fees were unwarranted.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the District Court abused its discretion by denying attorney fees under the private attorney general doctrine, as they successfully vindicated important constitutional interests against an unconstitutional bill passed with willful disregard for constitutional obligations.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the District Court did not abuse its discretion in denying attorney fees, contending the case was a 'garden-variety' constitutional challenge not deserving of fees and that legislative immunity applied.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the District Court's decision to deny attorney fees and remanded the case for calculation of attorney fees, finding that the District Court abused its discretion.

title: Barrett v. Montana
description: Whether three legislative bills (HB 349, HB 112, and § 2 of SB 319) unconstitutionally infringe upon the Montana Board of Regents' authority to supervise, coordinate, manage, and control the Montana university system.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs, members of the university community, argued that the bills were unconstitutional because they usurped the Board of Regents' exclusive constitutional authority over the university system and caused them individualized harm.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the plaintiffs lacked standing to challenge the bills and that HB 112 was a valid exercise of legislative authority, while implicitly conceding the unconstitutionality of HB 349 and § 2 of SB 319 by not defending them on appeal.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the District Court's decision that the plaintiffs had standing and that HB 349, HB 112 (as applied to higher education), and § 2 of SB 319 were unconstitutional infringements on the Board of Regents' authority, permanently enjoining their enforcement. The Court also affirmed the denial of attorney fees due to a lack of majority opinion on that issue.

title: State v. Gibbons
description: Whether the mandatory minimum $5,000 fine imposed by § 61-8-731(3), MCA (2019), without regard to a defendant's ability to pay, is facially unconstitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the mandatory minimum fine statute is constitutional and does not violate Gibbons's due process rights or right to effective assistance of counsel.
defendant_argument: Gibbons argued that the mandatory minimum fine statute is facially unconstitutional because it does not allow for consideration of a defendant's ability to pay, violating the right to be free from excessive fines.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Gibbons's DUI conviction but reversed the $5,000 mandatory minimum fine, holding that § 61-8-731(3), MCA, is facially unconstitutional because it prevents trial courts from considering constitutionally required proportionality factors like a defendant's ability to pay.

title: Montanans Securing Reproductive Rights v. Knudsen
description: Whether the Attorney General's proposed ballot statement for Constitutional Initiative 14 (CI-14) was argumentative, prejudicial, and inaccurate, and whether the petitioners' proposed ballot statement should have been approved.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that the Attorney General's proposed ballot statement for CI-14 was argumentative, prejudicial, and inaccurate, and that their own proposed statement was clear, impartial, and should have been approved.
defendant_argument: The Attorney General argued that the petitioners' challenge was statutorily foreclosed, and that their proposed ballot statement was deficient for failing to inform voters about changes to existing law, undefined terms, and implications for medical malpractice standards.
decision_outcome: The court accepted the petitioners' request for declaratory judgment, rejected the Attorney General's ballot statement for CI-14, and certified its own compliant ballot statement to the Secretary of State.

title: Forward Montana v. State
description: Whether the District Court abused its discretion by denying attorney fees to the Appellants under the private attorney general doctrine, with Appellants arguing the denial was an abuse of discretion and the State arguing it was not.
plaintiff_argument: The Appellants argued that the District Court abused its discretion by denying them attorney fees under the private attorney general doctrine after they successfully challenged unconstitutional sections of Senate Bill 319.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the District Court did not abuse its discretion in denying attorney fees, citing statutory immunity and claiming private enforcement was unnecessary.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the District Court's decision and remanded the case for the calculation of attorney fees for the Appellants.

title: Montana Democratic Party  v. Jacobsen
description: Whether four Montana laws (HB 506, HB 176, HB 530, and SB 169) that restrict absentee ballots for 17-year-olds, eliminate election day registration, ban paid third-party ballot collection, and revise voter ID requirements are unconstitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the four laws unconstitutionally interfered with or burdened the fundamental right to vote, disenfranchising various groups including young voters, Native Americans, and students.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the laws were constitutional, aimed at clarifying election laws, reducing administrative burdens, ensuring election integrity, and improving voter confidence.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the District Court's decision, holding that all four challenged laws (HB 506, HB 176, HB 530, and SB 169) are unconstitutional.

title: Monforton v. Knudsen
description: Whether the Attorney General correctly determined that Ballot Initiative #2 (BI2) was legally insufficient because it violated the separate-vote requirement of the Montana Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the Attorney General erred in concluding BI2 violated the separate-vote requirement, contending that the proposed amendments were closely related and concerned a single section of the constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that BI2 was legally insufficient because it proposed multiple, unrelated changes to the Montana Constitution as a single amendment, thereby violating the separate-vote requirement and risking voter confusion and logrolling.
decision_outcome: The court denied the petitioner's request to overrule the Attorney General's legal sufficiency determination and affirmed the Attorney General's rejection of BI2.

title: Stand Up Montana v. Missoula County Public Schools
description: Whether school districts' mask mandates during the COVID-19 pandemic violated students' and parents' constitutional rights, including substantive due process, privacy, and individual dignity, or if they were a legitimate public health measure.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the mask mandates infringed upon students' and parents' fundamental rights, including privacy, individual dignity, and parental rights to control their children's care, characterizing masks as medical treatment.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the mask mandates were a legitimate governmental interest aimed at slowing the spread of COVID-19 and ensuring a safe learning environment, and were rationally related to that interest.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the District Court's summary judgment in favor of the School Districts, concluding that the mask mandates did not violate the Appellants' substantive due process rights and that the exclusion of hybrid witness testimony was proper.

title: State v. Hinman
description: Whether the retroactive application of the Sexual or Violent Offender Registration Act (SVORA) violates the prohibition against ex post facto punishment in Article II, Section 31, of the Montana Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the amended SVORA requirements are not punitive and can be retroactively applied, consistent with prior precedent in State v. Mount.
defendant_argument: Hinman argued that the amended SVORA requirements are punitive in nature and their retroactive application violates the ex post facto clause of the Montana Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the District Court's order, holding that the amended SVORA is punitive and cannot be retroactively applied to defendants whose convictions predate the amendments, thus dismissing Hinman's charge.

title: State v. Noli
description: Whether the District Court erroneously concluded that the justification for the initial warrantless traffic violation stop ripened into a particularized suspicion of illegal drug activity within the lawful confines of the justification for the stop.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the initial traffic stop lawfully ripened into a particularized suspicion of illegal drug activity, justifying the prolonged detention and search.
defendant_argument: Noli argued that the traffic stop was unlawfully prolonged and expanded into a drug investigation without objective reasonable particularized suspicion, and therefore the evidence found should be suppressed.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the District Court's denial of Noli's motion to suppress the illegal drug evidence and her subsequent conviction, holding that the traffic stop was unlawfully prolonged.

title: Weems v. State
description: Whether the State of Montana's law restricting abortion care providers to physicians and physician assistants violates a woman's fundamental right of privacy to seek abortion care from a qualified health care provider of her choosing.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the statute unconstitutionally restricts a woman's fundamental right to privacy by limiting abortion providers, as Advanced Practice Registered Nurses (APRNs) are qualified to perform early abortion care without presenting a medically acknowledged health risk.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the statute codified previous rulings, that early abortion care by APRNs presents a health risk, and that the State has the authority to regulate for public health and safety.
decision_outcome: The Montana Supreme Court affirmed the District Court's order, ruling that the state law restricting abortion care providers to physicians and physician assistants is an unconstitutional interference with a woman's right of privacy to seek medical care from a qualified provider of her choice.

title: A.J.B. v. Montana Eighteenth Judicial District Court
description: Whether § 41-3-306(7)(b), MCA, which excepts cases subject to the Indian Child Welfare Act (ICWA) from eligibility for emergency protective services hearings in dependent-neglect cases, violates the constitutional right to equal protection of the law.
plaintiff_argument: A.J.B. argued that § 41-3-306(7)(b), MCA, is unconstitutional as it violates equal protection and due process rights by denying Indian children's families the right to an emergency protective services hearing, treating them less favorably than non-Indian families.
defendant_argument: The District Court argued that the issue was moot because the five business days for an emergency protective services hearing had passed and took no position on the constitutionality of the statute beyond its procedural argument.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court accepted and granted the petition for a writ of supervisory control, reversed the District Court's order, and ruled that the State shall not enforce § 41-3-306(7)(b), MCA, finding it unconstitutional.

title: State v. Staudenmayer
description: Whether the trial court violated Staudenmayer's constitutional right to confrontation by admitting clerk's minute entries into evidence without cross-examination, and whether the trial court abused its discretion by denying his motion to continue the trial date.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the minute entries were admissible as nontestimonial public records and that the trial court's denial of the continuance was within its discretion and did not prejudice the defendant.
defendant_argument: Staudenmayer argued that the minute entries were testimonial hearsay, violating his confrontation right, and that the trial court abused its discretion by denying his motion to continue, which prejudiced his defense.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Staudenmayer's bail-jumping conviction, finding no violation of his confrontation right and no abuse of discretion in denying the continuance.

title: State v. Larson
description: Whether the District Court erred by failing to suppress evidence confiscated by a group home manager, who subsequently turned the evidence over to police, or if the manager acted as a private party with authority to seize the items.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the group home manager, Jacquez, was a private party, not a state actor, and had the authority to confiscate Larson's electronic devices based on the group home's rules and Larson's consent, thus the evidence should not be suppressed.
defendant_argument: Larson argued that Jacquez became a state actor when police asked her to turn over his electronic devices, making the seizure warrantless and unlawful, and that Jacquez lacked third-party authority to consent to the seizure of his property.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the District Court's denial of Larson's motion to suppress, ruling that the group home manager acted as a private party and Larson had consented to the confiscation of his electronic devices by agreeing to the group home rules.

title: State v. Mefford
description: Whether the warrantless search of Bradley Mefford's phone by his parole officer was lawful under the consent or probation search exceptions to the warrant requirement, with Mefford arguing it was unlawful and the State arguing it was permissible.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the parole officer's search of Mefford's phone was reasonable and justified under either Mefford's consent or as a valid probation search.
defendant_argument: Mefford argued that the parole officer's search of his phone was unlawful because it exceeded the scope of his consent and lacked reasonable cause under the probation search exception.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the District Court's order denying Mefford's motion to suppress and dismiss, vacating his conviction and sentence.

title: McDonald v. Jacobsen
description: Whether the referendum proposed by HB 325, which requires Supreme Court justices to be elected district-by-district rather than statewide, is constitutional and ripe for judicial resolution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that HB 325 is facially unconstitutional based on prior judicial precedent (Reichert) and would deprive Montanans of their right to vote for each Supreme Court seat, making the issue ripe for judicial review.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the constitutionality of HB 325 was not ripe for judicial review because it had not yet been approved by voters, and alternatively, that its provisions were not unconstitutional and distinguishable from prior precedent.
decision_outcome: The Court affirmed the District Court's ruling, finding HB 325 facially unconstitutional and enjoining the Secretary of State from placing it on the November 2022 general election ballot.

title: Meyer v. Knudsen
description: Whether the Attorney General's determination that proposed ballot initiative I-33 was legally deficient was correct.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the Attorney General's rejection of I-33 was incorrect and overstepped his authority by applying an appropriation restriction meant for legislative initiatives to a constitutional amendment initiative.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the constitutional provision limiting initiatives that appropriate money should also apply to constitutional amendment initiatives, and I-33 constituted an appropriation, making it legally deficient.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the Attorney General wrongly rejected the proposed ballot initiative I-33, vacated the rejection, and ordered the proposal returned to the petitioner for signature gathering.

title: State v. Wellknown
description: Whether the District Court erred by denying Wellknown's Batson objection to a peremptory challenge, allowing improper prosecutorial remarks during closing arguments, and relying on an allegedly unconstitutional prior conviction to enhance his DUI conviction to a felony.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the peremptory strike was race-neutral, the prosecutor's closing remarks did not violate Wellknown's right to a fair trial, and Wellknown's prior DUI conviction was constitutionally valid for sentence enhancement.
defendant_argument: Wellknown argued that his equal protection rights were violated by the peremptory strike of a minority juror, his right to a fair trial was violated by the prosecutor's improper closing remarks, and his sentence enhancement was based on an unconstitutional prior DUI conviction.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the District Court's judgment and sentence, ruling against Wellknown on all three issues.

title: Advocates for School Trust Lands v. State
description: Whether House Bill 286 is facially unconstitutional for creating a presumption against State ownership of ground water diverted from private property for use on leased school trust land, thereby reducing the value of those lands, and whether an as-applied challenge to the bill would be futile.
plaintiff_argument: Advocates argues that HB 286 is facially unconstitutional because it violates the State's trust obligations under the Enabling Act and the Montana Constitution by relinquishing State ownership of water rights on school trust lands, thereby reducing the value of those lands.
defendant_argument: The State argues that HB 286 is constitutional and does not impair Montana's sovereign trustee duties or trust land management prerogatives to ensure that trust lands are not devalued, and that Advocates' challenge was unripe and futile.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the District Court's order denying leave to amend and awarding judgment in favor of the State, finding HB 286 facially constitutional and the proposed amendment futile.

title: Associated Press v. Usher
description: Whether the District Court erred in applying the statutory definition of a meeting to the Associated Press's Article II, Section 9 right to access a gathering of Judiciary Committee members.
plaintiff_argument: The Associated Press argued that a private gathering of legislative committee members, even without a quorum, should be considered a public meeting subject to the constitutional right to public access, and the statutory definition requiring a quorum should not override this right.
defendant_argument: Barry Usher argued that the private gathering did not constitute a "meeting" under the statutory definition because a quorum was not present, and therefore, it was not subject to open meeting laws or the constitutional right to public access.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Montana affirmed the District Court's order, denying the Associated Press's motion for judgment on the pleadings and granting Barry Usher's motion to dismiss.

title: State v. Peoples
description: Whether the District Court erroneously denied Peoples's motion to suppress evidence seized in a warrantless probation search of his apartment based on asserted violations of Article II, Sections 10 - 11 of the Montana Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the warrantless entry and search of Peoples's apartment were lawful under the probation search exception because there was reasonable cause to believe he violated his probation conditions.
defendant_argument: Peoples argued that the warrantless search of his apartment was constitutionally unreasonable, a pretext for a broader law enforcement investigation, and conducted in an unreasonable manner.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the District Court's denial of Peoples's motion to suppress, ruling that the warrantless entry and probation search were lawful.

title: State v. Smith
description: Whether law enforcement officers violated an individual's reasonable expectation of privacy by conducting a warrantless investigation on private property after being told to leave.
plaintiff_argument: Smith argued he had a reasonable expectation of privacy in his driveway, and the officer's continued warrantless investigation after being told to leave violated his constitutional rights.
defendant_argument: The State argued Smith had no reasonable expectation of privacy, implied consent for entry, and exigent circumstances (hot pursuit) justified the warrantless investigation.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the lower court's judgment, ruling that evidence obtained after the officer was told to leave Smith's residence must be suppressed.

title: McLaughlin v. Montana State Legislature
description: Whether the Montana Legislature's subpoenas to the Judicial Branch are valid, or if they are impermissibly overbroad and exceed legislative authority by seeking confidential and private information not related to a valid legislative purpose.
plaintiff_argument: Beth McLaughlin sought to quash and permanently enjoin the enforcement of the subpoenas, arguing they were overbroad, exceeded legislative authority, and sought confidential information and information in which third parties have a constitutionally protected individual privacy interest.
defendant_argument: The Montana Legislature argued it has the authority to obtain information for its legislative functions under the Montana Constitution and that its subpoenas serve a valid legislative purpose, including investigating judicial branch records retention, use of state resources for lobbying, and statements by judges.
decision_outcome: The court quashed the subpoenas issued by the Montana Legislature to Beth McLaughlin and the Department of Administration, finding them invalid, impermissibly overbroad, and not serving a valid legislative purpose, and denied the Legislature's motion to dismiss.

title: State v. Staker
description: Whether the District Court erroneously concluded that Staker had no reasonable expectation of privacy in text messages sent unknowingly to an undercover federal agent posing as a sex worker under an internet advertisement.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Staker had no objectively reasonable expectation of privacy in his text messages to an undercover agent, therefore no constitutional search occurred.
defendant_argument: Staker argued that the warrantless use of an undercover officer to induce his response and ensuing text message conversation violated his right to privacy under Article II, Sections 10-11 of the Montana Constitution.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the District Court's denial of Staker's motions to suppress the text messages and dismiss the resulting charge of patronizing prostitution.

title: Brown v. Gianforte
description: Whether Senate Bill 140, which abolishes the Judicial Nomination Commission and changes the process for selecting judicial nominees, violates Article VII, Section 8(2) of the Montana Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Petitioners argue that SB 140 is unconstitutional because it abolishes the Judicial Nomination Commission and replaces it with a process that lacks proper vetting and does not ensure the selection of qualified nominees, thereby violating Article VII, Section 8(2) of the Montana Constitution.
defendant_argument: Defendant argues that SB 140 is constitutional, as the Legislature has the discretion to determine the manner of judicial nominee selection, and the new process, including public comment and Senate confirmation, provides sufficient vetting.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that Senate Bill 140 does not violate Article VII, Section 8(2) of the Montana Constitution.

title: State v. Smith
description: Whether the District Court erred in admitting the victim's taped forensic interview and allowing the prosecutor's closing arguments, and whether the lifetime GPS monitoring condition is facially unconstitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the victim's forensic interview was admissible as a prior consistent/inconsistent statement, the prosecutor's closing arguments did not constitute plain error, and the lifetime GPS monitoring statute is constitutional.
defendant_argument: Smith argued that the victim's taped forensic interview was inadmissible hearsay, the prosecutor's closing arguments amounted to plain error, and the lifetime GPS monitoring requirement is facially unconstitutional.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Montana affirmed Smith's conviction and sentence, including the lifetime GPS monitoring condition.

title: State v. Lamoureux
description: Whether the Privacy in Communications statute is facially overbroad or a content-based restriction on speech, and whether it was correctly applied regarding the target of the threat and jurisdiction.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the Privacy in Communications statute is constitutional, not overbroad, and not a content-based restriction on speech, and that Lamoureux's conduct fell within its prohibitions, establishing jurisdiction and proper application.
defendant_argument: Lamoureux argued the Privacy in Communications statute is unconstitutionally overbroad, a content-based restriction on speech violating free speech rights, and that the court erred in applying it to threats made about a third party and when the recipient was out of state.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Lamoureux's convictions for three felony counts of Privacy in Communications.

title: Clark Fork Coalition v. Montana Department of Natural Resources & Conservation
description: Whether "legal demands" under the Montana Water Use Act (MWUA) include compliance with Montana Water Quality Act (MWQA) nondegradation standards, and whether the MWUA's limitation on who can object to water quality issues violates the constitutional right to a clean and healthful environment.
plaintiff_argument: The term "legal demands" in the MWUA should include MWQA nondegradation standards, and the MWUA provision limiting who can object to water quality issues violates their constitutional right to a clean and healthful environment by denying an adequate remedy for environmental protection.
defendant_argument: The MWUA's definition of "legal demands" is narrow and does not encompass MWQA nondegradation standards, and the MWUA's objection limitations do not violate constitutional rights because other statutes (MMRA, MWQA, MEPA) provide adequate remedies for environmental review.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the District Court's judgment, ruling that "legal demands" do not include MWQA nondegradation standards and that the MWUA's objection limitations do not violate constitutional environmental rights, thereby affirming the DNRC's decision to grant the water use permit.

title: State v. Keefe
description: Whether the District Court erred in resentencing a juvenile offender to life without parole by failing to appoint an independent expert, by finding him irreparably corrupt without considering rehabilitation evidence, and by not submitting the incorrigibility determination to a jury.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the District Court did not err in denying Keefe his own expert or a jury determination on incorrigibility, and that it adequately considered the evidence for finding Keefe irreparably corrupt.
defendant_argument: Keefe argued that the District Court erred by denying him his own expert, by finding him irreparably corrupt without considering rehabilitation evidence, and by not allowing a jury to determine his incorrigibility.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the District Court's decisions on expert appointment and jury determination but reversed its finding that Keefe was irreparably corrupt due to the failure to consider rehabilitation evidence, remanding for a new sentencing hearing.
